markdown:
Accounting hiring is shaped by the calendar more than most functions. Month-end close, quarter-end reporting and the annual audit all create deadlines that decide when people can interview, when new hires are productive and when experienced staff start looking elsewhere. This guide pulls together four things accounting leaders usually ask about separately: how to measure hiring, how to scope the main roles, which skills are changing and what keeps people on the team.

It does not publish industry averages. An earlier series of articles on this site quoted precise time-to-fill, compensation and attrition figures without naming a source we could stand behind, so we removed them. Where a number appears below, it is an illustrative example with its assumptions stated, or it points you to a public source to check yourself.

## How should an accounting team define its hiring metrics?

Write each definition down and keep it fixed for the year. Most disagreements about "slow hiring" turn out to be two people counting different things.

| Metric | A clear definition | Where it usually goes wrong |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Time-to-fill | Days from an approved requisition to an accepted offer | The clock stops at the start date, which folds notice periods into recruiting |
| Offer acceptance | Accepted offers divided by written offers | Verbal offers and counteroffers are left out |
| Source of hire | The channel that produced the person who accepted | Credit goes to the last click, not the first real contact |
| 90-day attrition | Hires who leave within 90 days divided by hires in that period | Internal transfers are mixed in with external hires |
| Cost per hire | Direct recruiting spend divided by hires, agency fees shown separately | The cost of an unfilled seat is ignored |

Compare yourself with a cohort that resembles you: the same level (staff, senior, manager, controller), a similar company size and the same market. If you use an outside source, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational data or a professional body survey, record the publisher, the year and how they define each term before you compare.

## What does an open accounting seat really cost?

Cost per hire counts what you spend to recruit. It leaves out what the vacancy costs while the work waits. In accounting that usually shows up as slower close, overtime for the people covering and delayed reconciliations.

Vacancy cost = direct recruiting cost + cost of cover per day x days open.

Here is an illustrative example. These inputs are assumptions chosen to keep the arithmetic easy, not market data.

| Assumption | Value used |
| :--- | :--- |
| Direct recruiting cost for a senior accountant | $6,000 |
| Cover cost (overtime or contract help) | $250 per day |
| Days the seat is open | 70 |

On those inputs the cover cost is $17,500 and the vacancy cost is $23,500. Cutting the open period to 50 days lowers the cover cost to $12,500. Substitute your own payroll and contractor rates before using the method in a business case.

## Which accounting roles are hardest to scope, and what should you decide first?

Titles overlap across companies, so decide the scope of the seat before you write the brief. These are the roles that most often get mis-scoped.

- **Senior accountant.** Decide whether the seat owns reconciliations and journal entries or also technical memos, new-standard adoption and audit support. These are different hires.
- **Accounting manager or assistant controller.** Clarify how many direct reports, who owns the close calendar and whether the person reviews the work of offshore or outsourced providers.
- **SEC and financial reporting manager.** Only relevant if you file. Specify the filings the person has prepared before, not just "SEC experience."
- **Controller at a mid-market or sponsor-backed company.** State the systems migration, audit history and reporting cadence the controller inherits. Candidates price these into their decision.
- **Tax manager.** Separate compliance from provision and planning. A candidate who has done only one will struggle in a seat that needs both.
- **Cost or plant accountant.** Name the inventory and costing method in use; the skill transfers poorly between methods.
- **Internal audit and SOX lead.** Say whether the seat designs controls, tests them or manages the external auditor relationship.

Compensation for each of these varies by metro area, company size and credentials. Rather than copy a number from a roundup, build a range from three sources: your own current pay bands, a public dataset such as the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, and the offers you have lost. Revisit the range when you see a pattern of declines on pay.

## Do you still need to require the CPA?

For attest work and many reporting seats a license is a legal or practical requirement. For other seats it is a habit. Ask what the license is protecting. If the answer is technical competence in revenue recognition, lease accounting or consolidation, you can test that directly with a work sample. State licensure rules and alternative pathways differ by state and are changing, so check your state board rather than assuming. Dropping a blanket requirement for non-attest roles widens the pool; keeping it where the work needs it protects you.

## Which skills are changing, and which still matter?

Three shifts come up in nearly every conversation with accounting leaders.

**Automation of matching and reconciliation.** Transaction matching, accrual suggestions and variance commentary are increasingly drafted by software. The work that remains is deciding which exceptions matter, explaining them and fixing the process that produced them. Screen for judgment about exceptions, not speed at tick-and-tie.

**Data fluency.** Being comfortable with SQL, a BI tool or a scripting language helps accountants trace a number back to its source. You rarely need an engineer; you need someone who can query the ledger without waiting for a report.

**ERP and close tooling.** Candidates who have configured or migrated a cloud ERP, or run a close checklist tool, bring knowledge that is hard to teach quickly. Mention your stack in the job post; people decide partly on tooling.

Skills that are losing value are the ones software already does well: manual matching, copy-paste spreadsheet roll-forwards and rote tax data entry. They still need to be understood, but they should not be the centre of a job description.

For assessment, replace trivia tests with a short, realistic work sample: a messy reconciliation with two planted errors, or a draft memo with a questionable conclusion. Ask the candidate to find the problem and explain how they would stop it recurring.

## Why do accountants leave, and what helps?

The reasons people give are consistent across firms. Treat them as hypotheses to test with your own exit and stay interviews.

- **Close-cycle compression.** If every month-end repeats the same late nights, people leave in the quieter weeks. Fix the cause, such as late sub-ledger cut-offs, before adding perks.
- **Pay that lags the market.** Annual reviews can leave experienced staff below what a new hire is offered. A mid-year check against current offers is cheaper than a replacement search.
- **No visible path.** Manager roles are limited. A technical track, such as a technical accounting lead, gives strong individual contributors somewhere to go.
- **Tooling friction.** Staff who spend their days exporting and reformatting data become frustrated. Removing one recurring manual reconciliation is a retention action.
- **Reactive management.** A regular one-to-one that asks "what is slowing you down?" does more than an annual survey.

Run a short post-close retrospective each month: what went late, why and who owns the fix. Run a stay conversation each quarter with your most important people, and write down what they say.

## How should onboarding fit the close calendar?

New hires who start in the middle of close are often left alone. Schedule start dates just after close where you can, give a new accountant one contained process to own in the first month and name a buddy who is not their manager. Compare 90-day attrition by start week once you have a year of data; you may find the calendar matters.

TaaSFlow is a recruiting platform with managed execution. Agents source and score candidates against the criteria you approve. A recruiter reviews every shortlist before you see it.
